summary:
Observed in FS.GG.Algorithms (ALGO-01.2, FS-GG/.github#5224) and re-measured on Fable 5.18.0, Node v26.11.1 and .NET 10.0.403.

**The behaviour.** F# evaluates a `for` loop's bounds once, before the first iteration. For **unit-step loops in either direction**, Fable instead writes the limit into the JavaScript loop condition, so it is re-evaluated before every iteration:
- `for _ in a .. b` emits `for (let i = a; i <= b; i++)`;
- `for _ in a .. -1 .. b` emits `i >= b`;
- `for i = a to b` and `for i = a downto b` do the same.

A limit with a side effect runs repeatedly: 4 calls against 1 on .NET for a 3-iteration loop. More importantly, **the iteration count changes when the limit reads state the loop body mutates**. `let mutable remaining = 3` with `for _ in 1 .. remaining do remaining <- remaining - 1` runs 3 times on .NET and 2 times under Node.

**Not affected:** the lower bound (`for _ in f () .. 5` evaluates `f` once), and general stepped ranges (`for _ in 1 .. 2 .. f ()` iterates `rangeDouble(1, 2, f())`, evaluated once).

**How it showed up.** A cross-runtime fixture decoder wrote `for _ in 1 .. reader.ReadU32() do`. Under Node it consumed extra input and failed; .NET was correct. The Fable proof caught it only because its compile gate fails closed (see `fable/compile-gate-must-check-exit-status`) and both runtimes' outputs are compared byte for byte.

**Rule for Fable-portable code.** Never put a side-effecting or body-mutated expression in the limit of a unit-step `for` loop. Bind the limit to an immutable local first (`let n = reader.ReadU32()` then `for _ in 1 .. n do`). Audit existing portable code for `for ... in a .. f ()`, `.. -1 .. f ()`, `to f ()` and `downto f ()`.

**Scope.** Measured on Fable 5.18.0 for JavaScript only. The other Fable targets were not checked. An upstream issue draft, `docs/upstream/fable-for-range-bound.md` in FS.GG.Algorithms, is for Root to file. The draft cited below is the first version; FS.GG.Algorithms#28 narrows its scope to unit-step limits, as stated here.
title: Fable re-evaluates the limit of unit-step for loops every iteration, so the iteration count can differ from .NET
